title: Flat Base Breakout
teaches: The flat base breakout as we trade it: a leader rests in a box near its highs above the 50-day and 200-day, the pivot is the base's highest high, the buy is the trade through it at market in regular hours, the stop sits a few cents under the breakout day's low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and a loss taken at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: One, two or three weeks do not get the job done.
facts.claim: IBD: one, two or three weeks do not make a base.

facts.quote: The stock's price declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to intraday trough.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.

facts.quote: The correction within a flat base should be no more than 15% from its intraday high to the bottom of the pattern.
facts.claim: IBD: the correction inside a flat base is no more than 15%.

facts.quote: It should look like a rectangular box with a correction from high to low of no more than 15%.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base looks like a rectangular box.

facts.quote: the "flat" base has kind of a "U" shape and doesn't look so flat.
facts.claim: IBD allows a flat base with a slight U shape.

facts.quote: Flat bases should show tight trading.
facts.claim: IBD: flat bases should show tight trading.

facts.quote: These shallow patterns often start forming as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance.
facts.claim: IBD: a flat base forms as a stock rests after an earlier advance.

facts.quote: In a weekly chart, look for periods of sideways movement or mild declines following a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price.
facts.claim: IBD: look for sideways movement after a prior uptrend of at least 30% (stated for any base).

facts.quote: The typical buy point is the price high made before the decline, plus 10 cents.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is the high before the decline plus 10 cents.

facts.quote: To get the proper buy point, add 10 cents to the highest price in the pattern, which is usually the start of the base.
facts.claim: IBD's buy point is 10 cents above the highest price in the pattern, usually the start of the base.

facts.quote: The buy point in a flat base is 10 cents above the left-side high.
facts.claim: IBD: the flat base buy point is 10 cents above the left-side high.

facts.quote: Sometimes you can draw a trend line connecting at least three points along the top of the base and find the lowest potential entry.
facts.claim: IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top of the base.

facts.quote: you want to see volume bulge at least 40%-50% above average when a stock breaks out of the flat base.
facts.claim: IBD wants breakout volume at least 40% to 50% above average.

facts.quote: A breakout needs to produce a gain of at least 20% in order to be counted as one stage.
facts.claim: IBD: a breakout counts as a stage only if it gained at least 20%.

facts.quote: Breakouts from late-stage bases will often blow up.
facts.claim: IBD: breakouts from late-stage bases often blow up.

facts.quote: It's usually best to buy when a stock breaks out from a first-stage or second-stage base.
facts.claim: IBD: it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base.

facts.quote: One guideline is the 7%-8% sell rule.
facts.claim: IBD's general loss limit is the 7% to 8% sell rule.

facts.quote: Flat bases form over a 5 to 65 week range. The minimum depth is 0% with a maximum of 15%.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base is 5 to 65 weeks long and 0% to 15% deep.

facts.quote: Flat bases often occur after a stock runs up after breaking out of one of the other chart patterns.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: flat bases often follow a run-up out of another pattern.

facts.quote: In the case of a Cup, Flat Base, Consolidation or IPO Base, the Pivot corresponds to the Left Side High that began the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: a flat base's pivot is the left-side high that began the base.

facts.quote: In most cases, it is the highest intra-day price over the last 100 days (or 20 weeks)
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the left-side high is usually the highest intraday price of the last 100 days.

facts.quote: The percent decline from the start of the base (left side high) to the bottom (intraday low) of the base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith measures depth from the left-side high to the base's intraday low.

facts.quote: Stocks emerging from third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: third, fourth or later stage bases are late and more likely to fail.

facts.quote: The Base Stage and Count are always reset to 1 once an intraday low price undercuts the low of the previous base.
facts.claim: MarketSmith: the base count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.

facts.quote: The Pivot Range is 0% to 5% above the pivot point
facts.claim: MarketSmith's buy range is 0% to 5% above the pivot.

facts.quote: A prior uptrend of 30% or more: This is the initial strong move that leads into the consolidation phase.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a prior uptrend of 30% or more leads into the base.

facts.quote: the stock's price should not fall more than 15% from its highest point within the base.

facts.quote: the trading volume should be at least 40% higher than its average volume (1.4 times the relative volume).

facts.claim: TraderLion: a well-formed flat base is tight and orderly.

facts.claim: TraderLion: flat base breakouts do better in a strong, bullish market.

facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day and no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.claim: A13: the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

facts.claim: Our stop may move up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell.

walkthroughs.title: NUS, September 2013: the textbook shelf
steps: NUS, September 2013. The stock nearly doubled, then shelves six weeks, riding the rising 10 and 21-day. Three taps of 90.
Context and pattern check out: above its 50-day and 200-day, shallow at 10.3%, tight, a flat ceiling. The pivot is 90.
2013-09-09: it trades through 90 on 1.9x volume. Buy at market, 90.01. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 88.22.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base, stop taken next day. Instead it reaches 3R the next session. We hold.

walkthroughs.title: ALLY, June 2019: tight at the end
steps: ALLY, 2019. A leader rests 11.2 weeks after a 31% run, only 5.5% deep: the shallowest base of the ten.
Four taps of 30, and inside days into the breakout. That is tight at the end, the rule in one picture.
2019-06-27: it clears 30 on 1.80x volume. Buy at market, 30.28. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 29.79.
Failure mode: a close at the low, back in the base. Instead it grinds to 3R on day 10. Slow still pays.

walkthroughs.title: WSM, September 2023: the throwback and the trims
steps: WSM, 2023. An 8-week shelf, 14.6% deep, four taps, after a 30% run. On 2023-09-25 it breaks out on 4.99x volume.
Buy at market, 73.16. Stop under the day's low, 72.24. 3R comes the next day, too soon to sell.
5R by day 10: time for the first sell. Then a throwback to 71.56, through the pivot and the original stop.
Failure mode: a close back inside the base. It came after the first sell; the trail rode the run to 99.

questions.q: What kind of base is this leader resting in?
choices: A boxy rest near highs after a run
A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash
A pole that doubles in a few weeks
A drift under the falling 200-day
questions.answer: A boxy rest near highs after a run
questions.why: A boxy rest near the highs after a run. IBD says a flat base should look like a rectangular box, and it forms as a stock takes a breather after an earlier advance. A V-shaped bottom comes after a crash, and a drift under the falling 200-day is a downtrend. We buy the breather because only it gives a clear top to buy through and a stop that can sit close.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base is a leader catching its breath in a box near the highs.

wrong.A V-shaped bottom after a hard crash: That is a bottoming pattern after a drop. A flat base rests near the highs after an advance.
wrong.A pole that doubles in a few weeks: That is a flag's pole. A flat base is the rest, not the run.
wrong.A drift under the falling 200-day: Below the 200-day we do not buy. A flat base sits above its averages, near its highs.

questions.simple: We buy a flat base because a strong stock resting in a box near its highs gives a clear top and a close stop.
questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the right side of the chart, where the stock has paused near its highs.

questions.q: Where is this flat base's pivot, the level it must trade through?
choices: The base's highest intraday high
The base's lowest intraday low
The rising 50-day average
The midpoint of the base
questions.why: The base's highest intraday high. The top of the box is where sellers have turned the stock back again and again. A trade through it means buyers just won that fight, so that is where we buy. MarketSmith calls it the left-side high that began the base. IBD adds 10 cents to it, which does not matter with a market order. The lowest low is the floor, and the 50-day is support inside the base.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is the top of the box. Mark it before the open.

wrong.The base's lowest intraday low: That is the base low, the floor. The breakout goes through the ceiling.
wrong.The rising 50-day average: The 50-day is support inside the base, not the trigger.
wrong.The midpoint of the base: Halfway up the box is still inside the box. Nothing has broken out.

questions.simple: The pivot is the top of the box, because sellers keep stopping the stock there and a trade through it shows buyers won.

deeper.counter: IBD quotes its buy point 10 cents above the high. We mark the high itself and buy at market as price trades through it. It is the same setup. Only the line you watch sits 10 cents lower.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the top edge of the box, the level price keeps running into.

questions.q: On a flat base breakout the stop goes a few cents under the base low.
questions.why: False. The stop goes a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card the breakout day has price above the 50-day and the ___-day, and the 50-day sits above that line.
questions.why: 200. On the breakout day price is above the 50-day and the 200-day, and the 50-day is above the 200-day. The rulebook also bars longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. The 50-over-200 order is our own setup test.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 50, above the 200, and the 50 over the 200. Then look at the box.
questions.simple: The blank is 200, because price must sit above the 50-day and the 200-day with the 50 above the 200.

questions.q: When do you buy?
choices: Trade through the pivot, regular hours
At the first daily close above the pivot
In premarket, if it gaps over the pivot
Inside the base, just under the pivot
questions.answer: Trade through the pivot, regular hours
questions.why: As it trades through the pivot in regular hours, bought at market. Set the alert at the pivot and let the trade come to you. Waiting for the close means a higher fill, and the stop stays put, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Premarket is out because no new buys come outside regular hours. Buying inside the base has no trigger, and Kullamagi finds anticipating less effective.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the pivot. Alert at the pivot, market order, regular hours.

wrong.At the first daily close above the pivot: Our trigger is the trade through the pivot, not the close. A close entry pays more, so the stop sits farther away and the size shrinks.
wrong.In premarket, if it gaps over the pivot: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.Inside the base, just under the pivot: That is anticipating with no trigger. Kullamagi finds it less effective; we wait.

questions.simple: Buy with a market order as price trades through the pivot, because waiting for the close means a higher fill and a smaller size.
questions.story: The day before a breakout.

questions.q: Volume that dries up in the second half of the base lifts the grade, but we do not need it to buy.
questions.why: True. Volume that dries up helps the grade, but a base without it can still trigger. Bulkowski finds volume inside a rectangle trends down 70% of the time, so it is common and does not promise a better result. In our scan of past flat bases, the ones where volume dried up did about the same as the rest.
questions.lesson_line: Volume that dries up is a plus, not a must.
questions.simple: True, because volume that dries up is common and did not make our past flat bases work better, so it only lifts the grade.

questions.q: Our card wants a flat base to be the first or second base since the last stage reset.
questions.why: True. Our card wants the first or second base since the last stage reset. IBD says it is usually best to buy a first-stage or second-stage base. MarketSmith says third, fourth or later stage bases are late in their moves and may be more likely to fail. The count resets to 1 when price undercuts the prior base's low.
questions.lesson_line: Count the bases. The first two are the ones we want.
questions.simple: True. Our card wants the first or second base, because later bases are late in their move and may fail.

questions.q: Strong sales and earnings count for more than the chart.
questions.why: False. We prefer stocks with growing sales and earnings, but the chart comes first. The chart shows what buyers and sellers are doing now, and it gives the entry and the stop. Growth helps you choose between two good charts. It does not rescue a bad one.
questions.lesson_line: Numbers help. The chart decides.
questions.simple: False, because the chart gives the entry and the stop, and growth only helps you choose between good charts.

questions.q: Where does this flat base start?
choices: At the left-side high
At the lowest low of the base
At the first 50-day crossover
On the day of the breakout
questions.why: At the left-side high, the highest price just before the rest began. MarketSmith and IBD both call it the start of the base. Depth and the pivot are both measured from there, so it decides where you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Find the left-side high first. Everything else is measured from it.

wrong.At the lowest low of the base: The low is the bottom of the box, found later. The base starts at its first high.
wrong.At the first 50-day crossover: The 50-day is a line inside the base, not its start.
wrong.On the day of the breakout: That is where the base ends, not where it starts.

questions.simple: A flat base starts at the left-side high, because the buy point and the depth are both measured from it.
questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the high the stock made just before it started resting.

questions.q: That picture is a base that is tight at the end. What does it do for the trade?
choices: Keeps the stop close to the buy
Warns that the base is about to fail
Makes the breakout run farther
Lets us buy before the pivot
questions.answer: Keeps the stop close to the buy
questions.why: It keeps the stop close to the buy. Small daily ranges put the day's low near the pivot, so the stop sits near the buy. A close stop lets the same risk buy more shares. IBD says flat bases should show tight trading. ALLY showed it in one picture, with four taps of 30 and inside days into the breakout. Its stop sat 1.6% under the buy.
questions.lesson_line: Tight at the end keeps the stop close. Inside days into the pivot are the picture.

wrong.Warns that the base is about to fail: Tight trading is a good sign. IBD says flat bases should show tight trading.
wrong.Makes the breakout run farther: A tight base does not promise a bigger run. It keeps the risk small.
wrong.Lets us buy before the pivot: Buying inside the base has no trigger. The buy is still the trade through the pivot.

questions.simple: Tight bars keep the stop close to the buy, and a close stop lets the same risk buy more shares.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the last ten bars at the right edge of the chart. Most days trade in a narrow range, and an inside day, one that trades inside the day before, shows up near the end.

questions.q: Price has stalled at about the same top three times. What does that repeated stall give you?
choices: A clear level to buy a break through
A level to place your stop under
Proof that the stock will break down
A reason to buy before it breaks out
questions.answer: A clear level to buy a break through
questions.why: A clear level to buy a break through. Each stall is sellers turning the stock back at the same price, so the top is a line you can watch and set an alert on. A trade through it is the first sign buyers won. IBD draws a line across at least three points along the top, and Bulkowski wants the top touched at least three times. Our scan found three taps no better than two, so more taps make a cleaner picture and are not a must.
questions.lesson_line: A top that holds again and again is a line to watch. The trade through it is the buy.

wrong.A level to place your stop under: The stop goes under the day's low, not under the top. The top is where we buy.
wrong.Proof that the stock will break down: A stall proves nothing. Stalls at one price only mark the line to watch.
wrong.A reason to buy before it breaks out: Buying inside the base has no trigger. The stalls say sellers are there, so we wait for the break through.

questions.story: The day before a breakout. A stock rests 6.4 weeks under about 733. Look at how many times it has run into that same top.
questions.simple: Repeated stalls at one price draw a clear line, and a trade through it shows buyers won, so that is where we buy.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's rectangle wants one line touched at least three times and the other at least twice, using distinct peaks and valleys. Our scan found three clean taps no better than two, so we treat more taps as a cleaner picture, not a rule.

questions.q: A close under the 200-day before the trigger ends the flat base setup.
questions.why: True. A close under the 200-day before the trigger ends the setup. The 200-day separates a long-term uptrend from a downtrend, and a rest under it is a pause in a decline, not a leader catching its breath. The rulebook bars longs below the 200-day, unless it is a parabolic long. A brief shakeout under the 50-day is different, and we allow it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there is no flat base to buy.
questions.simple: True, because under the 200-day a stock is in a downtrend, and a rest there is not a leader catching its breath.

deeper.trap: The two lines are not treated alike. A brief shakeout under the 50-day is allowed inside a base. A close under the 200-day is the rulebook's hard line, and it ends the setup before the trigger.

questions.q: At the breakout the stock is 2% over its pivot and 12% above its 9 EMA. Our rule?
choices: Skip it; it is too stretched
Buy; the pivot is what matters
Buy at half the usual size
Buy, but with a tighter stop
questions.answer: Skip it; it is too stretched
questions.why: Skip it. A long more than 10% above its 9 EMA is too stretched to buy, and at 12% this one is past the line, even though it is only 2% over the pivot. A stock that far above its average can fall back toward it, and a drop that size would blow through a stop that normally sits within about 3% of the buy. The pivot is the trigger, but it does not override the stretch rule. Half size and a tighter stop do not change the answer.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout that is already stretched is a chase with a different name.

wrong.Buy; the pivot is what matters: The pivot is the trigger, not the whole rule. The stretch rule still applies at the fill.
wrong.Buy at half the usual size: Size does not fix a stretched entry. The rule is skip.
wrong.Buy, but with a tighter stop: A tighter stop does not fix a stretched entry either. The rule is skip.

questions.simple: Skip it, because a stock this far above its 9 EMA can fall back and blow through our stop.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We never buy a flat base breakout more than ___% above the pivot.
questions.why: 4%. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point. MarketSmith's buy range runs 0% to 5% above the pivot, so our line is stricter. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the pivot and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The blank is 4, because we never buy more than 4% above the pivot.

deeper.trap: The 5 in the bank is the trap. MarketSmith's range runs to 5% above the pivot, a looser vendor line. Our rulebook cuts it to 4%. Past that, a late buy leaves the stop farther away, so the share count shrinks.

questions.q: A flat base stop is a real stop order with the broker, not a level you watch yourself.
questions.why: True. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. A level you watch depends on you being at the screen and willing to sell when it hits. The order sells for you when you are away or frozen.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head is a debate. A stop with the broker is an appointment.
questions.simple: True, because a stop in your head works only if you are watching and willing to sell, and an order does not wait.

questions.q: A ten-week base about 11% deep, a level top tapped five times, one range held. What is it?
choices: A flat base, still resting
A VCP, shrinking swings
A cup, handle forming
A double bottom forming
questions.why: A flat base. It holds one range under a level top, and IBD says a flat base should look like a rectangular box. A VCP's pullbacks tighten one after another instead. A cup is a rounded fall and recovery with a handle. Telling them apart matters because each has its own buy point and stop.
questions.lesson_line: One range, one ceiling, the same floor: that is the box. Tightening swings are the other setup.

wrong.A VCP, shrinking swings: A VCP tightens pullback by pullback. These swings hold one range.
wrong.A cup, handle forming: A cup is a rounded U that falls well below the top, then dips again for a handle. This base is boxy.
wrong.A double bottom forming: A double bottom makes two separate lows. This base holds one range under a level top.

questions.simple: A flat base holds one range under a level top, so it has a clear buy point, unlike a VCP or a cup.
questions.story: The day before a breakout. Look at the swings over the last ten weeks.

questions.q: IBD's buy point is the base's high plus 10 cents; our market order at the trade-through makes the 10 cents moot.
questions.why: True. IBD adds 10 cents to the left-side high for its buy point. We mark the high itself and buy at market as price trades through it. So the 10 cents does not matter to us.
questions.lesson_line: Same level, no 10 cents. The pivot is the high; the trigger is the trade through it.
questions.simple: True. IBD adds 10 cents to its buy point, but our market order as price breaks through makes that gap not matter.

questions.q: Buy the breakout today?
choices: No; wait until it has reported
No; wait one more day, then buy
Yes; the trigger fired this morning
Yes, but at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; wait until it has reported
questions.why: No. We make no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. The trigger fired Monday, but the report comes Wednesday after the close, inside that window. A report can gap the stock past your stop overnight, so the loss can be far bigger than the one you planned. A trade already open is held through a report only if it is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A breakout two days before earnings is a coin flip with a story. Wait.

wrong.Yes, but at half the usual size: Size does not fix a report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.No; wait one more day, then buy: Tuesday is still inside the 3 days before the report. The window runs up to the report.
wrong.Yes; the trigger fired this morning: The trigger fired, and the calendar still says no. The earnings rule is a hard line.

questions.story: The base is clean and tight. The pivot is 112.00 and it trades through this Monday morning. Earnings come after the close on Wednesday.
questions.simple: No, because a report can gap the stock past our stop, and this one comes Wednesday, inside the 3 days.

deeper.trap: The rule is about the date, not the setup. A clean base, a strong trigger or a smaller size do not lift it. It also covers new buys only. A trade already open is held through a report only if it is already up 5R.

questions.q: When does the first sell usually come?
choices: Day 3 at the earliest, into strength
A fixed third at 3R, on day one
Half of it, the day after the buy
All of it as soon as it hits 1R
questions.answer: Day 3 at the earliest, into strength
questions.why: Day 3 at the earliest, into strength. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1, because a winner usually runs for several days and a sale that early gives up most of that push. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. WSM was up 3R on day 1 and reached 5R by day 10.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment. Wait until day 3 at the earliest, then sell into the push.

wrong.A fixed third at 3R, on day one: That was the old rule. The first sell is a judgment, and day 1 is very rare.
wrong.Half of it, the day after the buy: Selling that early is rare. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.All of it as soon as it hits 1R: That sells far too early. The first sell waits for a push, often at about 5 to 10R.

questions.simple: The first sell is a judgment, and we wait until day 3 at the earliest because a winner often runs for several days.
questions.story: Bought on the breakout and already up 3R the next session.

questions.q: One R is the fill minus the stop. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 75.92. One R is the fill minus the stop: 73.16 minus 72.24. Add three of those to the fill, 73.16, and you get 75.92. It is a mark on the ruler and not a fixed sell. WSM passed both 3R and 5R on the buy day itself.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It is a measuring mark, not an automatic sell.
questions.simple: 3R is the fill plus three times the gap between the fill and the stop, which is 75.92.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.$75.00: Added the three R to the stop instead of the fill.
wrong.$70.40: Subtracted the three R instead of adding them.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 73.16 with the stop at 72.24.

questions.q: An RS rating of 85 (how well a stock beats the others) in one of the weakest groups still makes a leader.
questions.why: False. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. A rating of 85 in a weak group does not meet it, because the group is not being bought, and a breakout needs buyers behind it.
questions.lesson_line: A flat base in a laggard is a box going nowhere. Buy the leaders.
questions.simple: False, because a leader needs strong buying in its group too, and a strong rating alone in a weak group is not enough.

questions.q: In an Orange market, which of these may you buy?
choices: Only the A+ base, and no other
All three, each at full risk per grade
None of them; Orange means all cash
The A+ and the A, but not the B
questions.answer: Only the A+ base, and no other
questions.why: Only the A+ base. The market filter is the app's guide to how much the account should trade. Orange is a weaker market, so we take only A+ setups, the ones we judge cleanest, because a clean setup has the best chance when the market is not helping. Green is full risk per grade and up to 10 positions, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Red is mostly cash and shorts. TraderLion finds flat base breakouts are more likely to succeed in a strong, bullish market.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the box. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.None of them; Orange means all cash: Mostly cash is Red. Orange still allows the best setups.
wrong.The A+ and the A, but not the B: Orange allows only A+. The A setup waits too.
wrong.All three, each at full risk per grade: That is Green: full risk per grade. Orange narrows you to the A+ setups.

questions.simple: In Orange we take only A+ setups, because a weaker market only rewards the cleanest charts.
questions.story: The app's market filter has four readings: Green, Yellow, Orange and Red. It tells us how much the account trades. Green is the most open reading and Red the most closed. Today it reads Orange, one step from Red. We also grade every setup A+, A, B or B-. A grade is our judgment of how clean the setup looks, with no checklist, and it sets the size. You have three flat bases ready to trigger, graded A+, A and B.

questions.q: What is the trade now?
choices: The floor reclaim as a setup
A breakout through the old top
Nothing; the stock is broken
A short, with a stop over 71
questions.answer: The floor reclaim as a setup
questions.why: The floor reclaim, as its own setup. Our name for it is a U&R, an undercut and reclaim. Once the base low is undercut, the flat base is off. When price takes the floor back quickly, the dip shook out weak holders and buyers stepped in, so the trade is the reclaim with its own trigger and stop, not the breakout. How fast is a judgment call. Here the floor at 71 was undercut Tuesday and reclaimed by Thursday.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the floor and the box is gone. The reclaim is its own trade.

wrong.A breakout through the old top: The undercut ended the flat base. The old pivot is no longer this setup's trigger.
wrong.Nothing; the stock is broken: A quick reclaim is a shakeout, not a break. It is a different setup, not no setup.
wrong.A short, with a stop over 71: It reclaimed within two sessions. Shorting a quick reclaim is fighting strength.

questions.story: A nine-week flat base holds a floor at 71. Tuesday the low prints 70.40, under the floor. By Thursday the stock closes back above 71.
questions.simple: The trade is the reclaim, because the dip under the floor ended the flat base and price came right back.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ is not the stop; it can sit a whole base's depth away.
questions.why: The base low. It is not the stop, and it can be up to 15% away, the base's depth. That breaks our rule that the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the breakout day's low, not the bottom of the box.
questions.simple: The base low is not the stop, because it can sit up to 15% away, far wider than our usual stop.

deeper.trap: Two mistakes are named on the card. One is putting the stop at the base low, which is too wide. The other is pulling the stop tighter just to fit the size. Neither is the fix. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.

questions.q: The lowest low in the two months before the base was 40.00 and the left-side high is 50.00. The prior advance, in percent?
questions.why: 25%. The advance is the gain from the lowest low to the left-side high, divided by the low. 50 minus 40 is 10, and 10 over 40 is 25%. IBD looks for a prior uptrend of at least 30% in price. Kullamagi looks for a move of 30% to 100% or more in the past 1 to 3 months. A 25% run is under both lines.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the run before the rest. A box with no run in front of it is just a box.
questions.simple: The run is the gain from the low to the high, divided by the low, which is 25% here.

wrong.20%: Divided the gain by the high instead of the low.
wrong.125%: Forgot to subtract one: the high as a percent of the low.
wrong.10%: Read the 10 points of gain as 10 percent.

questions.q: Left-side high 100.00, the base's lowest intraday low 86.50. How deep is the base, in percent?
questions.why: 13.5%. Depth is the left-side high minus the base's lowest intraday low, divided by the high: 100 minus 86.5, over 100. MarketSmith measures it that way. IBD says a flat base declines no more than 15% from its intraday peak to its intraday trough.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low, divided by the high. Measure it; do not eyeball it.
questions.simple: Depth is the drop from the high to the low as a share of the high, which is 13.5% here.

reasons: computed key: the answer comes from arithmetic on the numbers given

wrong.15.6%: Divided the drop by the low instead of the high.
wrong.86.5%: Took the low as a percent of the high and skipped the drop.
wrong.1.4%: Decimal slip: moved the decimal one place.

questions.q: How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.08%. The gap between the 72.20 fill and the 70.70 stop is 1.50, and 1.50 over 72.20 is 2.08%. That sits inside the range our stops usually stay in, within about 3% of the buy. The distance matters because it sets the size: for the same dollar risk, a closer stop buys more shares and a wider one buys fewer. In our scan APH reached 3R on day 3.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop sits 2.08% below the fill, inside our usual 3%, and a closer stop lets the same risk buy more shares.

deeper.example: APH, trigger 2026-01-12: bought at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70, 2.1% away. The trade ran to 7.6R and reached 3R on day 3. The stop was set from the day's low first, and the size followed from it.

wrong.1.50%: Read the dollar gap as a percent.
wrong.20.80%: Decimal slip: moved the decimal one place.
wrong.0.02%: Stopped at the ratio and never multiplied by 100.

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 72.20 with the stop at 70.70.

questions.q: How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop: 30.28 minus 29.79. The gain is 32.73 minus 30.28. The gain divided by one R is 5R. We count in R because it measures a trade against its own risk, and our rules use it: the stop may move to breakeven between 2R and 5R, and a trade is held through earnings only when it is up 5R. ALLY took ten days just to reach 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is a mark on the ruler.
questions.simple: The gain is five times the fill-to-stop gap, so it is 5R, and R is how we compare trades of any size.

5R

questions.story: Bought on the breakout at 30.28, stop 29.79. One R is the gap between the two. Later it trades to 32.73.

questions.q: What now?

Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed
Widen the stop under the base low
Add to it; the price is lower
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is still the exit
questions.why: Hold it. A close back inside the base is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up, never down or wider. We set it before the trade, when we were calm, and one weak close is no reason to replace it. Here the day closed at 178.15, above the 178.10 stop. In the real AMZN case the next session's low took the stop, a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. The stop is the decision, and it was made before the open.

wrong.Widen the stop under the base low: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.Sell at tomorrow's open, it failed: A weak close is a warning, not an exit by itself. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Add to it; the price is lower: A weak close is a warning, not a reason to put more money in.

questions.story: You bought the breakout with the stop at 178.10. The day closes at 178.15, its low, back inside the base, just above your stop.
questions.simple: Hold, because the stop was set before the trade with a clear head, and one weak close is only a warning.

deeper.example: This is AMZN. The breakout day closed at 178.15, the low of its range, back inside the base, on 0.72x volume. The next session's low of 176.75 took the 178.10 stop. The weak close was the warning. The stop did the exit, as planned.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
Buy at market, stop at the base low
Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit
Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase
questions.answer: Buy at market, stop under the day's low
questions.why: Buy. 91.80 is inside our chase line: never buy more than 4% above the buy point. The stop stays a few cents under the breakout day's low. The base low is too wide, and pulling the stop in to fit the size is also a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Late is not too late. Inside the chase line, buy, and keep the stop under the day's low.

wrong.Buy at market, stop at the base low: The base low is not the stop. It can sit a whole base's depth away. The stop is a few cents under the breakout day's low.
wrong.Buy at market, stop pulled in to fit: Pulling the stop tighter to fit the size is a named mistake. The stop comes first and the size comes from it.
wrong.Pass; any buy past the pivot is a chase: The chase line is more than 4% above the buy point, not any price past it. 91.80 is inside the line.

questions.story: The pivot is 90.00. You missed the open. At 10:15 the stock trades 91.80.
questions.simple: Buy at market with the stop under the day's low, because 91.80 is inside the chase line.

deeper.trap: Passing feels safe, but the rule is a line, not a ban on late buys. Past 4% you skip it. Inside it you buy, and the stop stays under the day's low. Chasing costs size: the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink.
